en: I will support your idea in tomorrow's meeting.
tamil: நாளைக்கு மீட்டிங்ல நான் உங்க ஐடியாவை ஆதரிப்பேன்.
context: Promising support to a colleague.
explain: 'Will' is used for a promise or a decision made while speaking.
usage: Say it to a colleague who is nervous about sharing an idea.
leelaQ: How do you support a friend who has a new idea?
answer: I listen carefully and tell others why I think the idea is good.

en: What is better for your health, running or yoga?
tamil: உடம்புக்கு ஓட்டமா, யோகாவா எது நல்லது?
context: Asking for health advice.
explain: 'What is better...?' with two choices asks for a comparison.
usage: Ask a friend or a trainer who knows about fitness.
leelaQ: How do you keep yourself fit and healthy?
answer: I keep fit by walking every evening and doing some yoga.

en: To be honest, I enjoyed the book more than the movie.
tamil: உண்மைய சொல்லணும்னா, எனக்கு படத்தை விட புத்தகம் தான் அதிகமா பிடிச்சுது.
context: Comparing a book and its film.
explain: 'To be honest' introduces a frank opinion. 'More than' compares the two.
usage: Use it in a chat with friends about a book that became a film.
leelaQ: Do you enjoy books or movies more?
answer: I enjoy movies more because I can relax and watch with my family.

en: Can we please talk about this calmly?
tamil: நாம இதை அமைதியா பேசலாமா?
context: Cooling down a heated talk.
explain: 'Can we please...?' is a soft way to ask for a calm talk.
usage: Use it at home or work when a discussion becomes loud or tense.
leelaQ: How do you stay calm in an argument?
answer: I take a deep breath and speak slowly to stay calm.

en: You make a fair point about the traffic.
tamil: டிராஃபிக் பத்தி நீங்க சொன்னது நியாயமான கருத்து.
context: Accepting a point in a discussion.
explain: 'Make a fair point' is a polite way to say the other person is right.
usage: Use it when someone mentions a problem you had not considered.
leelaQ: What is the biggest traffic problem in your area?
answer: The biggest problem is too many two-wheelers near the main signal.

en: I believe honesty matters more than marks.
tamil: மதிப்பெண்களை விட நேர்மை தான் முக்கியம்னு நான் நம்புறேன்.
context: Sharing a belief about values.
explain: 'I believe' shows a deeper opinion. 'Matters more than' compares two values.
usage: Use it in a talk about values with students or colleagues.
leelaQ: What matters more to you, marks or honesty?
answer: Honesty matters more to me because people trust honest people.

en: Are you sure this is the best option?
tamil: இதுதான் சிறந்த ஆப்ஷன்னு உங்களுக்கு உறுதியா தெரியுமா?
context: Politely doubting a choice.
explain: 'Are you sure...?' lets you doubt something in a polite way.
usage: Use it when a friend is about to pay for something and you have doubts.
leelaQ: When do you ask 'Are you sure?' to someone?
answer: I ask it when a friend is about to make a big decision.

en: I have decided that the red shirt suits you better.
tamil: சிவப்பு சட்டை தான் உங்களுக்கு நல்லா இருக்கும்னு நான் முடிவு பண்ணிட்டேன்.
context: Helping a friend choose clothes.
explain: 'Suits you' means it looks good on you. 'Better' compares two shirts.
usage: Say it in a clothes shop when a friend cannot choose.
leelaQ: What colour suits you best?
answer: Blue suits me best because it looks good with my skin colour.

en: We cannot say that one is always better than the other.
tamil: ஒண்ணு எப்பவும் இன்னொண்ணை விட நல்லதுன்னு நாம சொல்ல முடியாது.
context: Giving a balanced opinion.
explain: 'Cannot say' is useful when the answer is not simple. 'Always' is the key word.
usage: Use it in a debate when both sides have good points.
leelaQ: Is one kind of food or travel always better than another?
answer: No, it always depends on the place, the time and the person.

en: Is anyone here against the new timing?
tamil: புது நேரத்தை யாராவது எதிர்க்கிறீங்களா?
context: Checking for disagreement in a group.
explain: 'Against' means you do not support something. This question invites honest views.
usage: Use it in a team meeting before you finalise a schedule.
leelaQ: How do you feel about the timing of your work or classes?
answer: I feel it is good, but a little earlier start would be better.

en: Suggest a good book for me to read this weekend.
tamil: இந்த வார இறுதியில் படிக்க ஒரு நல்ல புத்தகம் சொல்லுங்க.
context: Asking a friend for a book idea.
explain: 'Suggest' is a verb for giving a recommendation. 'For me to read' shows the purpose.
usage: Use it with a friend who reads a lot.
leelaQ: What book would you suggest to a beginner reader?
answer: I would suggest a short story book because it is easy to finish.

en: Who do you think will win the match tomorrow?
tamil: நாளைக்கு மேட்ச்ல யார் ஜெயிப்பாங்கன்னு நினைக்கிறீங்க?
context: Guessing a match result with friends.
explain: 'Who do you think will...?' asks for a prediction about the future.
usage: Use it in a friendly chat before a cricket or football match.
leelaQ: Which team do you think will win the next big match?
answer: I think our home team will win because the players are in good form.

en: Help me choose between these two sarees.
tamil: இந்த ரெண்டு புடவையில எதை எடுக்கறதுன்னு எனக்கு உதவுங்க.
context: Asking for help in a shop.
explain: 'Choose between' is used when you have exactly two things.
usage: Use it with a friend, a sister or a shop assistant when you cannot decide.
leelaQ: Who helps you when you cannot decide what to buy?
answer: My sister helps me because she knows my taste well.

en: Do you mind if I share a different idea?
tamil: நான் வேற ஒரு ஐடியா சொல்லலாமா, உங்களுக்கு ஓகேவா?
context: Politely disagreeing in a meeting.
explain: 'Do you mind if I...?' asks for permission politely before you disagree.
usage: Use it in a meeting when you want to give another view politely.
leelaQ: How do you share a different opinion politely?
answer: I say that I see their point, but I ask if I may share another idea.

en: I don't mind waiting, it is fine.
tamil: நான் காத்திருக்க தயார், பரவாயில்ல.
context: Showing that you are flexible.
explain: 'I don't mind' means 'it is okay for me'. It is a friendly, flexible phrase.
usage: Say it when a friend is late or when a host asks you to wait for a while.
leelaQ: How long can you wait for a friend without feeling upset?
answer: I can wait for fifteen minutes, but not more than that.

en: Could you tell me why you prefer village life?
tamil: கிராம வாழ்க்கை ஏன் உங்களுக்கு பிடிக்கும்னு சொல்ல முடியுமா?
context: Asking for someone's reason.
explain: 'Could you tell me why...?' is a polite way to ask for a reason.
usage: Use it when you are curious about a friend's lifestyle choice.
leelaQ: What do you like most about village life?
answer: I like the fresh air and the friendly neighbours in a village.

en: Could you let me know if you like this design?
tamil: இந்த டிசைன் உங்களுக்கு பிடிச்சிருக்கான்னு சொல்ல முடியுமா?
context: Asking a client for a reaction.
explain: 'Let me know' asks someone to tell you later. 'If' here means 'whether'.
usage: Use it with a client or a colleague after sharing your work.
leelaQ: What do you say when you need quick feedback from someone?
answer: I ask them to give me feedback by evening.

en: The second option is not as good as the first.
tamil: முதல் ஆப்ஷனை விட ரெண்டாவது அவ்வளவு நல்லா இல்ல.
context: Comparing two options with a negative.
explain: 'Not as good as' says one thing is weaker than another.
usage: Use it when you rank two choices, like two plans or two products.
leelaQ: What do you do when one option is not as good as the other?
answer: I choose the better one and keep the other as a backup.

en: Are you enjoying the new job more than the old one?
tamil: பழைய வேலையை விட புது வேலை உங்களுக்கு அதிகம் பிடிச்சிருக்கா?
context: Asking a friend about a job change.
explain: 'Are you enjoying...?' asks about a feeling in these days.
usage: Ask it when you meet a friend who changed jobs recently.
leelaQ: What do you enjoy most about your work?
answer: I enjoy working with friendly people and learning new things.

en: What makes you say that this place is expensive?
tamil: இந்த இடம் விலை அதிகம்னு நீங்க ஏன் சொல்றீங்க?
context: Asking for a reason behind a comment.
explain: 'What makes you say...?' politely asks why someone holds an opinion.
usage: Use it when you want to understand a friend's complaint without arguing.
leelaQ: What makes a place expensive in your opinion?
answer: A place is expensive when the food and rent cost more than normal.

en: Shall we ask the others what they think?
tamil: மத்தவங்க என்ன நினைக்கிறாங்கன்னு கேட்கலாமா?
context: Suggesting to include everyone.
explain: 'Shall we...?' is a friendly suggestion that includes the listener.
usage: Use it in a group when only a few people have spoken.
leelaQ: Why is it good to ask everyone's opinion in a group?
answer: It is good because everyone feels important and we get better ideas.

en: Should we wait for the others or start now?
tamil: மத்தவங்களுக்காக காத்திருக்கலாமா, இல்ல இப்பவே ஆரம்பிக்கலாமா?
context: Asking the group for a decision.
explain: 'Should we...?' asks for advice from the group. 'Or' gives two choices.
usage: Use it when a meeting or a lunch is late and some people are missing.
leelaQ: Do you usually wait for friends or start without them?
answer: I usually wait for a few minutes, and then I start.

en: I did not enjoy the game because it was too loud.
tamil: சத்தம் ரொம்ப அதிகமா இருந்ததால எனக்கு அந்த ஆட்டம் பிடிக்கல.
context: Giving a reason for disliking an event.
explain: 'Did not' + base verb makes a past negative. 'Because' gives the reason.
usage: Use it when friends ask why you left a match or a party early.
leelaQ: What kind of place do you not enjoy, and why?
answer: I don't enjoy crowded places because I feel tired very fast.

en: Please say it again, I want to understand your point.
tamil: மறுபடியும் சொல்லுங்க, உங்க கருத்தை நான் புரிஞ்சுக்கணும்.
context: Asking someone to repeat politely.
explain: This shows you are interested, not annoyed. It is a polite way to ask for repetition.
usage: Use it in a meeting or a class when you did not catch someone's idea.
leelaQ: What do you do when you do not understand someone's point?
answer: I ask them to repeat it slowly and give one example.

en: How was your trip compared to last year's?
tamil: போன வருஷ டிரிப்போட ஒப்பிட்டா இந்த டிரிப் எப்படி இருந்துச்சு?
context: Asking a friend to compare two trips.
explain: 'Compared to...' asks for a comparison. 'Last year's' means last year's trip.
usage: Ask it when a friend returns from a holiday they take every year.
leelaQ: How was your last holiday compared to the one before?
answer: It was better because the weather was nice and the hotel was good.
